items.title: Luis Conte interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 24, 2025
items.q: this is from your James Taylor bandmate, Lou Marini.

ctx.x: Yeah. Angel City Drum Works is the name of the company and they have like – I think I’m the only percussion player they have, but they have a lot of drummers. Erskine, Peter Erskine, JR, a bunch of cats. And they take us around in the studios. But the new world now is having a home recording studio you know. So I have one and thank God I’ve been pretty busy about it, with it. And a lot of sessions happen now that you don’t go anywhere, you just do them here. Overdubs.

Yeah. They send you a track and you can add. Yeah. I have another quote here. I’m sure the studio scene, as you mentioned, has changed a lot. And this is from your James Taylor bandmate, Lou Marini. And he was talking about the way songs are put together these days, and he said, “When I listen to these vocoder vocals and the rhythm tracks you could just as easily be listening to a washing machine. Luis Conte is a master percussionist. He’s always playing stuff for us from African tribal music, Caribbean,…

Totally agreed. Of course. Man, you know what I call – and I work on some of these, I could tell you some things that man, what are some of these, you know the modern music that you hear on the radio. It sounds like wallpaper music to me. That’s what I call it. I call it wallpaper music. It’s just wallpaper. It’s almost – you know do you notice the wallpaper? No? So, it doesn’t matter. There’s like a formula. And it’s not only sad man, you have this one artist becomes a huge hit, now you have every record company…

items.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023
items.q: When you consider like Luis Conte is always playing, because he’s such a master percussionist. He’s always playing stuff for us from like African tribal music or Caribbean or Brazilian

ctx.x: Oh, what a — I mean who couldn’t love Joe Wilder? Musically and personality-wise. And he described exactly what you were just saying, that there was so much work, he was on staff and he played the television orchestras. And then, even back then, he talked about “and then the synthesizer came in” and so I guess some things never change.

Yeah. Well you know it’s not the first time that musicians got out of work. When talking movies took over, overnight basically, within a year or so or a couple of years, thousands and thousands of gigs from guys playing in movie theaters just disappeared. So you know I listened — like I was listening to the soundtrack last night of a series, a contemporary Swedish series that I’m watching on Netflix. And I realized that these computer sounds, they’re just a part of our lives now you know. The atmospheric sounds…

Let me go back a bit — you said improvising is a mysterious art — a mysterious thing to do. When you play a solo, an improvised solo over a one or two chord vamp or a 12-bar blues, is what’s going on in your head different than what you would play on “Giant Steps”? Or even “Body and Soul.” In other words more chord changes — how do you negotiate the challenging chord changes of a song as opposed to a one chord vamp?
